[PAPER_0055, relevance_score=0.260] Moreover, following the findings of Nakayama et al.

In the present study, we attempted to obtain such converging evidence from spoken word recognition with Chinese-English bilingual and English monolingual listeners by testing this hypothesis. We expected to observe a phonological competition effect at the syllabic level in the Chinese spoken word recognition and the syllabic and phonemic competition effects in the English spoken word recognition for both Chinese-English bilinguals and their English monolingual counterparts, suggesting that bilingual listeners would recruit the appropriate phonological unit to accommodate their listening in different languages.

[PAPER_0063, relevance_score=0.286] Following this significant finding, we claimed that syllable position would also constrain phonological activation processes in Chinese disyllabic words owing to an inherently serial property of spoken words. Specifically, we predicted that word-initial information of Chinese disyllabic words (an overlap in the first syllable) should be weighted more heavily compared with word-final information (an overlap in the second syllable).

[PAPER_0070, relevance_score=0.353] Therefore, Experiment 2 was conducted to extend the findings of Experiment 1 from monosyllabic words to disyllabic words. In this experiment, we anticipated a significant CV competition effect for disyllabic words because Experiment 1 reported a significant CV competition effect for monosyllabic words using a similar mouse-tracking spoken word recognition paradigm. The experiment was preregistered on the Open Science Framework before data collection. The preregistration form together with the data files and detailed R scripts of the experiment can be found at https://osf.io/zm7cy.

The fastest response time data were trimmed using the absolute cutoff of 100 ms. [PAPER_0073, relevance_score=0.343] Stimuli

The experimental stimuli consisted of a total of 360 disyllabic Mandarin Chinese compound words (see Appendix B). All disyllabic target words were spoken by a male native Chinese speaker and digitally recorded at 16 bits with a sampling rate of 44,100 Hz by Praat in a soundproof booth. The average duration of the spoken target words was 1,512.9 ms (SD = 371.4 ms). The stimuli were divided into two sets based on the primary manipulation in this Experiment: character position.

[PAPER_0074, relevance_score=0.303] The competitors in the set either shared the same phonological units in the word-initial or word-final position with their targets. We thus created a total of four experimental lists (two lists shared the phonological units in the first character position, and the other two shared the units in the second character position) in which each target and its competitor shared phonological units in either the word-initial or word-final position. In Experiment 2, each participant randomly received one of the four lists. Each list had two blocks, in which each target word was presented one time in random order.

[PAPER_0088, relevance_score=0.338] Results

Block order (first block, second block), character position (word-initial, word-final), and condition (CV, CV control, C, C control) were simultaneously entered into the LMMs to examine how the three fixed factors affected the TRTs, MTs, error rates, MD, and AUC of mouse movements. In addition, we employed intercept-only random-effect structures (i.e., subject and item intercepts) in the LMMs.
